title: Microstate gardening — rough PRD and experiment notes
content:
Context:
This is a very rough personal sketch exploring an alternative to full session checkpoints for conversational applications — a "microstate gardening" approach. Idea: persist and maintain a compact set of small, composable deltas (microstates) rather than full transcripts or dense vectors per turn. Purpose is to support fast resume, efficient partial rehydration, and cheaper long-term storage while keeping latency predictable for tail requests.

Why bother / problem statement:
- Many customers keep long conversation histories to maintain persona/context. Storing and re-sending whole history increases token cost and latency.
- Full KV cache snapshots are large and expensive to store and restore for infrequently resumed sessions.
- Current heuristics (trim last N turns, summarize) are brittle and can lose important context. Need structure that:
  - Lets us reconstruct approximate conversational state quickly (small CPU work).
  - Keeps rehydration size small for most requests.
  - Allows targeted invalidation/refresh of parts of state when model or policy changes.

High-level proposal (microstate gardening):
- Represent session history as a chronologically ordered list of microstates. Each microstate is a tiny artifact (1–3 tokens of metadata + small structured payload) describing a discrete change: user preference update, slot set, entity mention, recent intent drift, small summary anchors, or compressed continuation hints.
- Microstates are typed and composable. Types: intent-hint, slot-update, named-entity-anchor, recent-turn-compress, semantic-anchor, system-action-ref, persona-tweak.
- Runtime can stitch N most-relevant microstates into a compact prefix to send to the model or use for reranking.
- Store microstates as append-only logs with cheap small-object storage and occasional compaction (gardening). Compaction rules merge older microstates into higher-level anchors (e.g., daily digest).

User scenarios / personas:
- Customer support bot with long multi-topic threads: needs to remember account flags (billing-suspended), last action, and a concise summary of prior troubleshooting steps.
- Productivity assistant with user preferences (tone=formal) that rarely change but must persist across months.
- Multi-session game-like experience where state changes frequently but only a few keys matter to next-turn generation.

User stories (examples):
- As a product user, I want the assistant to remember my saved preferred language and apply it without resending the entire corpus of past messages.
- As an app developer, I want resume latency to be <50ms extra overhead in 95th percentile for sessions resumed after >30 days.
- As infra engineer, I want storage cost per inactive session to be <10% of current snapshot-based approach.

Acceptance criteria / success metrics:
- Resume latency: 95p added latency from session lookup + microstate stitch <50ms on hosted infra baseline.
- Token cost reduction: average prompt tokens sent per resumed session reduced by >=40% across test suite.
- Storage delta: average bytes stored per inactive session reduced by >=60% relative to baseline dense snapshot.
- Quality: downstream NLU/RAG/LLM perplexity/accuracy on held-out prompts should degrade <=5% (task-specific) vs baseline.

Design considerations / components:
1) Microstate schema (minimal): id, type, timestamp, vector-hint-id (optional), small payload string (max 512 chars), confidence/score, refs (ids of other microstates).
   - Implementation: keep as newline-delimited small JSON in object store (cheap) or as rows in a wide-column store for quick scans.
2) Relevance scoring: when resuming, query most recent microstates and score by recency+type-weight+session-hard-constraints.
3) Stitching policy: token budget for stitched prefix (e.g., 150 tokens). Algorithm: greedily add highest-score microstates until budget hit, then emit minimal connective context.
4) Compaction (gardening): background jobs that merge many microstates into a summary anchor; rules configurable by customer (time-based, type-threshold, access-frequency).
5) Compatibility with KV cache and model change: microstate should map to KV cache priming heuristics; for model upgrades, mark microstates as needing re-eval (staleness flag) and optionally auto-recompute.

Trade-offs and risks:
- Risk: too aggressive compaction can lose nuance (e.g., multi-turn clarifications). Mitigation: preserve high-importance microstates (billing flags, auth tokens).
- Complexity: more moving pieces in storage/rehydration path — increases operational burden. Start opt-in for specific workloads to limit blast radius.
- Consistency: append-only with compaction means race conditions when multiple clients write microstates concurrently. Need idempotent ops and optimistic merge.

Experiment matrix (initial):
- P0 experiment: Proof-of-concept microstate store + stitcher for a single test bot. Compare resume latency and token cost vs naive transcript send. Measure quality via automated eval prompts.
- P1 experiment: Type weighting heuristics — A/B experiment across weighting profiles (recency-heavy vs type-priority).
- P2 experiment: Compaction aggressiveness — compare weekly vs monthly compaction and user-visible quality.

Data and metrics to capture:
- Time to fetch & stitch microstates (p50/p95/p99).
- Prompt tokens sent per resumed session.
- Bytes stored per session and storage cost delta.
- Quality metrics: answer relevance (human labels), rerank recall, hallucination rate on diagnostic prompts.

Rollout / migration plan (rough):
1) POC (2–3 sprints): implement microstate schema, simple append store, naive stitcher. Run on internal test bot.
2) Pilot (1–2 months): opt-in pilot for 5 customers (support bot, assistant, enterprise demo). Collect metrics, run manual QA.
3) Gradual opt-in: add console toggle + per-customer compaction policies. Provide migration tool to convert snapshots -> microstates (best-effort summarizer).
4) Full platform support: expose microstate API, SDK helpers, and UI to inspect microstates in Console.

Open questions / TODOs:
- How to securely reference secrets/state? (store flags vs pointers to secure store)
- What is the canonical microstate TTL for legal/regulatory requirements? Need product + privacy input.
- Precise schema limits: payload char limit, vector-hint size, indexing strategy.
- Storage cost model: blob store vs DB vs hybrid (small objects cheaper vs high request rates).
- UX for developers: how much control do we expose (manual microstate writes vs auto-generated hooks)?

Next steps (my personal checklist):
- [ ] Sync with Lena on compaction heuristics (this week).
- [ ] Draft tiny API surface for microstate write/read (do it as example SDK snippet).
- [ ] Run quick empirical test: take 1000 sample sessions, run greedy microstate extraction (naive rules) and measure token reduction.
- [ ] Add note to INF-7423 about privacy/retention questions and assign legal reviewer.

Notes / rough heuristics used in thinking:
- Prefer append-only + compaction for simplicity and offline batching.
- Budget for stitched prefix should be small (100-200 tokens) to get majority of quality wins.
- Keep microstates typed to avoid sending irrelevant bits (e.g., system logs).

Final thought (brain dump):
If this works, we can enable long-tail sessions cheaply: customers who want years of conversational continuity get compacted anchors + a handful of microstates, which enables personalized behavior without paying the token + latency premium of replaying entire transcripts. But we need to be cautious about subtle regressions in generation quality — experiments first.

Random notes to self:
- Think about integration with Optimize: suggest compaction thresholds based on observed token savings.
- Consider exposing a "peek" endpoint in Console to preview stitched prompt.
- Possible name variants: microstate gardening, micro-anchor architecture, incremental session compaction.

-- end --
